headline: Highest risk is prompt-injection and cascading-error via shared filesystem: Goose can write/read/execute with MCP, while PaddleOCR processes documents/images and may consume untrusted outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Goose can read/write the filesystem and use MCP, and its state is shared via filesystem; PaddleOCR processes documents/images that Goose could place there. That creates a plausible injection bridge if PaddleOCR outputs are later treated as instructions. No direct parser details are documented, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF Goose reads PaddleOCR output files from the shared workspace as instructions
IF PaddleOCR writes OCR text into files that Goose later ingests without sanitization
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Require explicit human review before Goose consumes OCR output
Prefix all OCR artifacts as data-only in filenames and headers
Disable automatic file-watching between agents
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose touches source code and files in cwd, with broad network egress and model-provider/extension tokens; PaddleOCR handles documents and images. If both share a workspace, sensitive document contents can flow from B into A's outputs or upstream APIs. The profiles do not show PHI or a guaranteed upload path, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or mounted workspace
IF Goose forwards file contents to configured model providers or MCP servers
mitigations: Use separate directories and mounts
Restrict Goose network egress to approved endpoints
Redact sensitive fields before OCR ingestion
Turn off automatic sync/export from shared folders
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss policies

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose has unrestricted filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and git-state modification; its shared-state model is via filesystem. PaddleOCR can run browsers and call APIs, so if both touch the same workspace, concurrent writes and stale reads can corrupt outputs or git state. Because the profiles do not document locking, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git repository
IF no external lock or serialization layer is enabled
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Pause one agent while the other writes git state
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Review and merge changes manually
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can generate code, shell actions, and MCP calls; PaddleOCR can turn documents/images into text that Goose may consume. That creates a default pathway where OCR errors or injected text become authoritative inputs for downstream actions. The profiles do not show autonomous email/commit authority, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Goose uses PaddleOCR output as source-of-truth without verification
IF downstream shell or MCP actions are triggered from OCR-derived text
mitigations: Require a verification step before acting on OCR text
Keep OCR output and action prompts in separate files
Add checksum or diff review before execution
Limit Goose to read-only mode for OCR review tasks
requires-engineering: implement confidence thresholds and human approval gates

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. Goose handles model-provider keys and extension tokens, while PaddleOCR handles documents/images, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated-data flow. I therefore rate only a low compliance risk from incomplete documentation.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is processed through either agent
IF deployment policies require residency or retention guarantees not documented here
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Document retention and deletion settings
Confirm vendor/data-processing terms before deployment
Log which agent touches which data class
requires-engineering: add compliance policy enforcement
